Given the limited availability of detailed data on occupancy, internal loads, and envelope characteristics, a prototype college building model developed by Oak Ridge National Laboratory (Bae et al. 2022) was used with EnergyPlus®, a whole-building energy simulation tool, rather than developing a custom model for a specific campus building. The prototype model representing typical characteristics of U.S. higher education buildings as classified in the 2012 Commercial Buildings Energy Consumption Survey (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2016), includes a functional mix of spaces like classrooms, laboratories, faculty offices, and support areas, each with distinct internal loads and occupancy schedules. While the original prototype complied with ASHRAE Standard 90.1, including mass wall construction, built-up roofing, and metal-framed windows (Bae et al. 2022), this study modified the building envelope to reflect pre-1980 construction standards (Deru et al. 2011), better matching the age and thermal characteristics of the UPR-RP campus. The heating, ventilating, and air-conditioning system was modeled as a variable air volume system served by a central gas boiler and electrically-driven water-cooled vapor-compression chillers, aligned with the existing chilled water infrastructure at UPR-RP. For climate input, TMY3 data at San Juan International Airport in San Juan (World Meteorological Organization # 785260) were used to represent local climatic conditions. These modifications and modeling inputs establish a realistic basis for generating hourly cooling load profiles for a representative campus building, which are used in the subsequent techno-economic analysis. Figure 14a shows the modeled hourly cooling loads generated for the prototype college building over the first 30 days of the year, and Figure 14b presents daily aggregated loads across the full annual simulation period. The hourly load profile showed strong weekday-weekend variation as well as strong diurnal variation. On weekdays (Monday through Friday), hourly peak loads reached approximately 1,200 kW during daytime, corresponding to active classroom and laboratory use. In contrast, weekend daytime hourly peaks were significantly lower, around 400 kW, reflecting reduced occupancy and minimal instructional activity. Similarly, the daily cooling energy profile in Figure 14b showed seasonal variability alongside the weekday-weekend trends. Despite a constant cooling set point throughout the simulation, the annual trend in cooling demand followed a similar pattern to the ambient temperature profile shown in Figure 14b. This pattern implies that ambient temperature contributed to seasonal variation, as maintaining a fixed indoor temperature required more energy on hotter days. However, the relatively small variation in moving average temperature (approximately 2°C–3°C) indicates that occupancy-driven internal heat played a more significant role. During the spring months (February and March), maximum daily cooling energy was slightly lower, around 12–13 MWh, likely due to milder temperatures and reduced cooling demand. From April through mid-June, maximum daily cooling energy increased to approximately 16–17 MWh, and during the summer, maximum daily cooling energy slightly decreased to around 15 MWh.
